playground.label: Toy proof-of-work miner (uses input)
playground.code:
import hashlib
prefix = input('Block data: ')
zeros = int(input('Leading zeros required: '))
nonce = 0
while not hashlib.sha256(f'{prefix}-{nonce}'.encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0' * zeros):
    nonce += 1
print(f'nonce {nonce} gives', hashlib.sha256(f'{prefix}-{nonce}'.encode()).hexdigest())

title: How Bitcoin works: one transaction from wallet to blockchain, checked against the whitepaper

nodes.label: Transaction
nodes.body: How Bitcoin Works follows one payment, Buying from an Online Store, and its Bitcoin Transactions section treats a transaction like a line in a double-entry ledger whose difference is the transaction fee (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Transaction part
nodes.body: Transaction Inputs and Outputs names the two sides of every transaction and what lies between them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Input
nodes.body: An input spends funds by pointing at an earlier output and carrying a digital signature from its owner that anyone can check (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: An input spends funds by referring to an earlier transaction's output and proving ownership with a digital signature.

nodes.label: Output
nodes.body: An output receives funds, and the outputs add up to slightly less than the inputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: an amount locked to an address
nodes.definition: An output receives funds; the outputs add up to slightly less than the inputs.

nodes.label: Transaction fee
nodes.body: The fee is never written down as such: it is the difference between inputs and outputs, collected by the miner who includes the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The fee is implied: the difference between the inputs and the outputs, collected by the miner.

nodes.label: Linkage
nodes.body: Transaction Chains, Making Change and Coin Selection show how transactions connect to one another (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Transaction chain
nodes.body: Alice's payment to Bob's Store spends an output of the transaction in which her friend Joe paid her, so each payment links back to earlier ones (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Each transaction's inputs spend earlier outputs, so transactions form chains back through history.

nodes.label: Making change
nodes.body: Buying an item that costs 5 bitcoins with a 20-bitcoin input sends 5 to the store and 15 back as change, not counting the fee, often to a new change address for privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: An output larger than the payment returns the rest as change to a new address of the payer.

nodes.label: Coin selection
nodes.body: Coin selection is the wallet's choice of inputs: aggregating many small ones or using one large one, a balance people also strike with cash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Wallets choose which inputs to spend, balancing many small inputs against few large ones, much as people handle cash.

nodes.label: Form
nodes.body: Common Transaction Forms names the shapes transactions usually take (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Simple payment
nodes.body: The most common transaction is a simple payment with one input and two outputs, one of them change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The most common form: one input, and two outputs - the payment and the change.

nodes.label: Consolidation
nodes.body: A consolidation transaction spends several inputs into one output, the real-world equivalent of exchanging a pile of coins for a single note (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Many inputs spent into a single output, like exchanging a pile of coins for one note.

nodes.label: Unit
nodes.body: Amounts can be fractional, down to a smallest indivisible unit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Satoshi
nodes.body: A bitcoin divides into units from the millibitcoin, a thousandth, down to the satoshi, a hundred-millionth, so a millibitcoin is 100,000 satoshis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The smallest unit: a bitcoin divides into 100,000,000 satoshis.

nodes.label: Payment request
nodes.body: Buying from an Online Store shows the invoice Alice's wallet scans (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: BIP21 URI
nodes.body: The invoice QR code encodes a URI defined in BIP21 with the address, the payment amount 0.01577764, the label Bob's Store and a message, so Alice never types an address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: the invoice encoded in the store's QR code
nodes.definition: A BIP21 URI carrying the address, amount, label and message, which the wallet reads so the payer never types an address.

nodes.label: Network
nodes.body: Constructing a Transaction and Adding the Transaction to the Blockchain follow the payment from Alice's wallet onto the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Propagation
nodes.body: A transaction does not need a central server: Getting the Right Inputs, Creating the Outputs and transmitting it are all done by the wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Transaction propagation
nodes.body: Once signed, the transaction is transmitted to the network and relayed by nodes until miners hold it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A signed transaction is transmitted to the network and relayed by nodes until it reaches miners.

nodes.label: Block explorer
nodes.body: Block explorers such as Mempool.Space let anyone look up a transaction or block - and a Bitcoin Overview warning says the operator may learn what you look up (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: a site that shows a transaction or block
nodes.definition: A block explorer looks up addresses, transactions and blocks - and may learn what you look up.

nodes.label: Blockchain
nodes.body: The blockchain is the authoritative journal of all transactions, produced by miners through competitive computation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Mining
nodes.body: The Bitcoin Mining section explains how transactions become part of that journal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Block
nodes.body: Transactions are bundled into blocks whose small header needs an enormous amount of computation to form correctly but little to verify (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: a bundle of transactions with a small header
nodes.definition: Transactions are bundled into blocks whose header is hard to form correctly and easy to verify.

nodes.label: Consensus rules
nodes.body: Miners can only earn honest income from blocks that follow all of Bitcoin's consensus rules, so they are incentivised to include only valid transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: the rules every block must follow
nodes.definition: Miners earn honest income only from blocks that follow all consensus rules, which keeps blocks valid.

nodes.label: Sudoku analogy
nodes.body: The course notes picture mining as a giant competitive sudoku - hard to solve, easy to verify, harder or easier by grid size, and restarted after each solution - an analogy the 3rd edition does not use (Altunel, 2021).
nodes.example: mining pictured as a giant sudoku
nodes.definition: An analogy from the course notes: hard to solve, easy to check, adjustable in size, restarted after every solution.

nodes.label: Security
nodes.body: Spending the Transaction shows how confidence in a payment grows over time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Confirmation
nodes.body: Each block on top adds a confirmation; Nakamoto's paper computes that an attacker with a tenth of the hash power catches up from six blocks behind with probability 0.0002428 (Nakamoto, 2008).
nodes.definition: Each block mined on top of the one containing a transaction is one more confirmation; more confirmations make reversal harder.

nodes.label: Genesis block
nodes.body: Every block links back through hundreds of thousands of blocks to block number 0, the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The first block of the chain, to which every block links back.

nodes.label: Unconfirmed transaction
nodes.body: A payment first shows as unconfirmed: propagated but not yet in a block, and blocks arrive every 10 minutes on average rather than on a timetable - the ten-minute misconception the course notes warn about (Altunel, 2021).
nodes.example: a payment propagated but not yet in a block
nodes.definition: Propagated to the network but not yet recorded in a block; blocks arrive every 10 minutes on average, not on a timetable.

nodes.label: Small payment acceptance
nodes.body: Selling a cheap item unconfirmed carries low double-spend risk, as coffee shops accept small card payments without a signature, while an expensive item justifies waiting for confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: a cheap item sold without waiting
nodes.definition: A merchant may accept a small payment unconfirmed because the double-spend risk is low, as coffee shops accept small card payments without a signature.

nodes.label: Semantics
nodes.body: The course theme of semantic technologies meets the chapter in its transaction chain (World Wide Web Consortium, 2013).

nodes.label: Provenance model
nodes.body: A chain of spends is a record of where each value came from - a provenance record (World Wide Web Consortium, 2013).

nodes.label: Provenance graph
nodes.body: W3C's PROV Ontology describes entities derived from other entities by activities and attributed to agents, which is exactly the shape of outputs spent by transactions signed by key holders (World Wide Web Consortium, 2013).
nodes.example: a transaction chain described in PROV-O
nodes.definition: A transaction chain is a provenance graph: outputs derived from outputs by transactions, attributed to key holders - expressible in W3C PROV-O.

nodes.label: Practice
nodes.body: The course notes point students to an interactive demonstration of the chain of hashes this chapter describes (Altunel, 2021).

nodes.label: Interactive demo
nodes.body: Seeing a hash chain break is more convincing than reading about it (Altunel, 2021).

nodes.label: Blockchain demo
nodes.body: Anders Brownworth's Blockchain Demo shows that changing one character in an earlier block invalidates every later block, which is what makes the journal tamper-evident (Altunel, 2021).
nodes.definition: An interactive page where changing one earlier block invalidates every later block's hash.

findings: Chapter 2 follows one real transaction - Alice paying Bob's Store - through wallet, network and blockchain: transactions as double-entry lines of inputs and outputs with an implied fee, transaction chains, change and coin selection, common transaction forms, constructing and propagating a transaction, mining that bundles transactions into blocks, and confirmations that make a payment harder to reverse as blocks pile up.

The chapter's claim that a payment becomes harder to reverse with each confirmation is quantified in Nakamoto's paper: for an attacker with a tenth of the hash power the probability of catching up falls from 0.2045873 at one confirmation to 0.0002428 at six, and a Python transcription of the paper's own procedure reproduces that table exactly.

For the course theme, a transaction chain - each input spending an earlier output - is a provenance graph, and W3C's PROV Ontology offers the vocabulary to describe it: entities derived from entities by activities, attributed to agents.
The Bitcoin Core software that full nodes run to verify every rule has continued to release after the book; its releases page lists 31.1 as the newest.

The owner's course notes for this chapter (2021, after the 2nd edition) surfaced topics now added to the deck, each checked against the 3rd edition: the invoice as a BIP21 URI, which the 3rd edition prints in full with a bech32 address where the notes had the older format; why ten minutes is an average and six confirmations a convention, with small payments accepted unconfirmed at low double-spend risk as coffee shops accept small card payments, from the 3rd edition's chapter 12; the notes' own analogy of mining as a giant competitive sudoku, kept and labelled as an analogy because the 3rd edition does not use it; and the Blockchain Demo the notes link to, verified reachable.
